title: The Joy of Watching Microbudget Films

commenti.body:
The best microbudget films I’ve seen are the ones made by Matt Farley and Charles Roxburgh. These are very local no-budget genre pastiche movies made around Manchester, NH using friends and family  of the filmmakers and they are a total delight. They have grown to be masters at knowing what tone to hit and how to use non-professionals and cheap sets in ways that are intentionally funny and campy without resorting to becoming too meta or “intentionally bad”.

The best starting point is probably Don’t Let the Riverbeast Get You!. After than maybe check out Magic Spot, Metal Detector Maniac and Heard She Got Married. Also Local Legends is a very heartfelt and funny autobiographical work about Matt and his working process that will be most effective to watch after seeing a few of the other films first.

I think my top two might be John Paisz's Crimewave, which is just an incredibly inventive Guy Maddin-esque exploration of being an artist in suburban Manitoba or Chameleon Street, which I can only describe as a black Catch Me if You Can (and similarly based on a "true" story), but way better, which has so many layers about performance and identity. I also love Hisayasu Sato's amazing erotic films that explore alienation and perversion better than anyone else.

In truth there are so many subcategories you could call microbudget that it's hard to know where to began, from Jonathan Caouette's Tarnation, a personal exploration of memory and family which is famous for making over $1 million on a $200 budget (yes that is the correct number of 0s) to all sorts of brilliant B-movie horrors like Frank Henenlooper's Basket Case.

Love those guys, also Matt Farley puts his personal phone number in Local Legends and my friends and I left a voice message to tell him how much we liked his movie, and he chatted with us for a while!

I'll also second the Important Cinema Club in general as a great place to learn about directors and genres that don't get a lot of coverage making microbudget films.

Thunder Road is right on that $200,000 budget number and is my favorite movie of 2018. Jim Cummings is amazing both behind and in front of the camera. Here is the [short film](https://vimeo.com/174957219) that won a jury prize at Sundance.

I really enjoyed Interplanetary and For a few zombies more by Chance Shirley.

> What inspires you in a film like this?

I like being surprised by narrative.

I like efficiency.

I like it when art takes chances and lets characters make mistakes.

Pathogen is amazing for exactly the reasons you describe. It was made by a teenage girl. The blu ray from AGFA (American Genre Film Archive) comes with a feature length about the making of Pathogen and it will up your alley because the parents documented every step of the production.

I don’t think anyone’s ever made a better microbudget film than Shane Carruth’s debut feature “Primer.” It’s a masterpiece of minimalist sci-fi that fully embraces the mundane nature of its bland suburban setting and limitations of its budget to create an atmosphere of mystery and menace that’s completely unique. By the end of the film’s runtime everything remotely normal and reassuring about the world of the story has been turned on its ear, including the remarkable way the film’s biggest twist and main premise transforms from something fascinating and opposed to the oppressive routine of their workaday tech jobs into just another job of work to keep up with on too little sleep.

Coherence. $50,000, shot over 3 days, minimal scripting for spontaneity. Solid acting and a very compelling concept make the movie. As you watch it you can get a sense that this was made by someone who at minimum had an extremely clear vision for what they wanted and knew how to attain it. 

In addition Resolution, and The Endless are both similar. Little to no CGI or effects. Just great writing and fascinating concepts. Can't say too much about them without diminishing the experience but I highly recommend you check them out.
Lol you literally stole the one I was going to say, but I couldn’t find the cost.

Weirdly enough, some of my favorite films tend to be microbudget films even if I recognize they aren’t as good as their counterparts.

The best example is my love for Scorsese’s Who’s That Knocking at My Door which is definitely not objectively better than say Scorsese’s Raging Bull, however, it is this passion and love and desire to make a film that seeps through the former more than it does the latter.

And, it is the fact that every microbudget film is as much a making-of documentary as it is a narrative film that really draws me in especially because I’m currently in that stage of life where I’m working on my own microbudget films.

Therefore, there is definitely this love that I have for them that supersedes what we traditionally see as quality because I see so much of my own life and experiences in them while also viewing them as important texts on how to achieve this seemingly impossible dream.

My recommendations are: Frankie Latina’s Modus Operadi, Eric Leiser’s Imagination, Evan Glodell’s Bellflower, Jim Van Bebber’s Deadbeat at Dawn, The Duplass Brothers’ The Puffy Chair, Richard Linklater’s It’s Impossible to Learn to Plow by Reading Books, Maya Deren’s Meshes of the Afternoon, Shirley Clarke’s Portrait of Jason, Don Hertzfeldt’s It’s Such a Beautiful Day, Chris Maker’s La Jetee and Sans Soliel, and, of course, Martin Scorsese’s Who’s That Knocking at My Door.

Also, if you are looking for more, be sure to check out a lot of Troma’s titles because they have a lot of great microbudget films. I mean stuff that most companies won’t even touch, so they’re a great resource that I use when looking for lower budget films.

I’d also recommend looking through DVD sections at pawnshops and other secondhand stores! I’ve been exposed to most of these films by chance when I was looking for DVDs, so it’ll definitely expose you to new types of cinema and all different kinds of films that I could’ve never found searching online for films.

Anyways, I hope this helps! Have a great day!

I also work in the film industry and I'm writing what will likely be my first feature. I also enjoy seeking out art / films that seem to be at the level of which I currently have the ability to produce. Many films you see at even bigger festivals don't have enormous budgets, far less than a million dollars and only a handful are what you'd consider "hollywood" films that come with hollywood sized resources.  


The film which made me pick up a DSLR and go... holy shit, I could actually go out and make this (I mean... not really but it definitely felt like that at the time), was Monsters by Gareth Edwards. Hearing him talk about how he just dipped to Central America with a tiny little crew and just shot the shit out every location blew me away. At the time it really made me enjoy the film on a different level and I started seeking out other micro budget films.
Meshes and Deadbeat are both outstanding!
